title: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
titleJa: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
summaryJa: It comes as some investors have become concerned about the amount of money being spent on AI infrastructure.
bodyOriginal:
Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
- Published
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.
The figures were revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year.
It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have come under pressure over concerns about the large amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure.
An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.
Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.
The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row.
Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.
Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.
Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.
In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by more than 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 9.4% and SK Hynix dropping 10.8%.
Tech-heavy indexes in the region were also down. South Korea's Kospi was 7.6% lower while Japan's Nikkei 225 fell by 4.8%.

- Published5 hours ago

- Published19 hours ago
The falls come after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.
Tan said at an conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".
There also been concerns over the safety of AI models.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns about the technology's safety.
The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.
Anthropic has also been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down.
The company has continued expanding globally, opening an office in Singapore on Wednesday.

title: Elon Musk says Trump is 'ultimately' responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's Starshield systems
titleJa: Elon Musk says Trump is 'ultimately' responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's Starshield systems
summaryJa: "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote.
bodyOriginal:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump was responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.
Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.
That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram. Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.
Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.
The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire.
Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.
Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.
— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

title: Oil falls as investors assess Mideast tensions, International Energy Agency's report
titleJa: Oil falls as investors assess Mideast tensions, International Energy Agency's report
summaryJa: Oil fell Thursday, as traders assessed attacks on ships passing through Hormuz, while digesting the International Energy Agency's latest monthly report.
bodyOriginal:
Oil fell Thursday as traders assessed potential supply disruptions following attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, while digesting the International Energy Agency's latest monthly report on the outlook of the oil market.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery dropped 1.66% to $104.31 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November fell 1.09% to $94.05 per barrel.
A Singapore registered ship was sunk in the critical Strait of Hormuz, which raised worries of a prolonged Mideast conflict. "Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday.
Iran, meanwhile, has said it is "counting the moments" until it can start striking U.S. warships.
The International Energy Agency in its oil report for October out Wednesday cautioned that constraints on diesel markets could continue well into the next year, with fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to derail a recovery in oil supply.
To help ease prices, the Trump administration is considering to ease sanctions on "shadow fleet" vessels which transports oil and petroleum products from countries such as Russia, Reuters reported.
The lack of progress between U.S.-Iran diplomatic track "leaves little immediate prospect of a full reopening of the waterway," said Firas Bechwaty, head of business development at online trading platform ICM late Wednesday.
"At the same time, Saudi crude continues to reach international buyers through alternative routes, while accelerated emergency stock releases by IEA members provide an additional buffer, preventing a sharp rise in prices, even as tensions remain elevated," Bechwaty noted.

title: Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO
titleJa: Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO
summaryJa: Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion as it prepares for a highly anticipated initial public offering reportedly slated for November, according to people familiar with the matter.
bodyOriginal:
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion as it prepares for a highly anticipated initial public offering reportedly slated for November, according to people familiar with the matter.
Revenue rose from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, with first-quarter revenue at $4.7 billion, the people said, adding that Anthropic said it was profitable on an adjusted basis in the third quarter.
The company also told investors it was cash-flow positive, generating $1.70 in revenue for every dollar spent on computing power during the third quarter, according to the Financial Times. Investors expect Anthropic to reach $110 billion in annualized revenue by year-end, according to The Wall Street Journal.
CNBC previously reported that the Claude maker planned to disclose its third-quarter financial results for the first time at a meeting with potential investors, including institutional investors, citing two people familiar with the matter.

title: SK Hynix shares plunge 10% amid Asia tech rout as Fed rate hike fears, AI funding worries mount
titleJa: SK Hynix shares plunge 10% amid Asia tech rout as Fed rate hike fears, AI funding worries mount
summaryJa: A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks deepened Thursday, with Asian chipmakers tracking Wall Street losses as concerns over further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, financing of artificial intelligence investments weigh on sentiment.
bodyOriginal:
A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks deepened Thursday, with Asian chipmakers tracking Wall Street losses as concerns over further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, financing of artificial intelligence investments weigh on sentiment.
South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged over 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 7.1%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.1%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 7.7% and Samsung SDI declined 6.8%.
In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest dropped 6.9%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 5.4%. Renesas Electronics declined 5.4%.
The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom.
Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity.
The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%.
Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust.
"Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note.
The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs.
"What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs.

title: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
titleJa: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
summaryJa: Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US.
bodyOriginal:
How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
- Published
A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres.
Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.
"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.
The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.
Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.
"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.
A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.
Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.
There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by, external Pew Research Center.
Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.
Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.
"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."
Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation.
"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."
That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.
Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".
His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.
The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.
During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.
Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.
"People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."
New national polling, external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy.
Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.
Yet, recent research, external from Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.
Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project.
Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.
Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.
In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.
Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls, external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials.
Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.
Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in a private memo, external that Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres.
"This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle", the NRSC added.
Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.
The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.
At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed.
Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".
It could play a part in the state's upcoming senate race too.
Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".
Many of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.
It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.
For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.
Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand.
"There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.
During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project.
"She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"

title: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
titleJa: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
summaryJa: With Christmas on the horizon, we trace children's toys from factories in China to US shelves.
bodyOriginal:
How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
- Published
On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".
Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external
Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external
With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.
As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.
The factory
Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.
In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.
The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.
Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.
Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."
Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.
So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.
On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.
Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.
Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.
He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."
And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.
Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report, external at the start of this year.
Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.
The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.
Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.
The ship
From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.
Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.
Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.
Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.
The US border
Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.
This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.
This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.
"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.
The US toy company
The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.
That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.
"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.
If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.
While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.
Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

title: OpenAI bugging suspect booked one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia with family before arrest
titleJa: OpenAI bugging suspect booked one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia with family before arrest
summaryJa: "Like countless Americans, Mr. Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream," his criminal defense lawyer said Wednesday.
bodyOriginal:
Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national charged with secretly installing a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI, had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest, federal prosecutors told a judge in a newly unsealed court filing.
Alfozan "has the means — and will have the incentive — to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested," the U.S. Attorney's Office in San Francisco said in the Oct. 8 filing, which asked a judge to seal a criminal complaint against him and a warrant for his arrest.
The filing said the tickets were booked for Oct. 12, from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul.
The judge granted the sealing request, and Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9, the Department of Justice has said.
He has been detained since his arrest.
Alfozan, 35, is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists a prince from that nation's ruling royal family as a fellow partner.
The VC firm, Raed Ventures, says on its website that Alfozan, who lives in the San Francisco area, "is a seasoned technology professional with deep experience in startups, entrepreneurship, and scaling tech companies."
"He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform," Alfozan's bio page on Raed's site says.
Raed, which focuses on investments in the Middle East, announced Alfozan had joined the firm on Feb. 8, 2025, two days after Raed said Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud had joined as a venture partner. A venture partner usually is a consulting or project-based role, not an investing partner or director who is responsible for raising funds or leading deals.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, according to the Department of Justice. The company said it terminated him this month.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that when Saudi tech influencers visited San Francisco in September, "it was Alfozan who welcomed them to OpenAI offices where he gave them tours."
A former CIA official with extensive experience in the Middle East, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the nature of their past work, told CNBC that Raed Ventures is "basically a state organ" of the Saudi government. One of Raed's funds in December 2024 received an investment from Saudi Venture Capital, a subsidiary of SME Bank, which is part of Saudi Arabia's National Development Fund.
In addition to being a venture partner in Raed, the prince, Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, is a member of the ruling Al Saud family, and the managing director and vice chairman of his family's private office, according to his bio on Raed's website.
The former CIA official said that if Alfozan's alleged bugging of OpenAI is part of a state-sponsored espionage effort, it shows that "in the AI and tech boom, even the kingdom of Saudi Arabia has assessed that the risk is worth the gain to engage in economic espionage against a close ally."
The former official also said this incident is "probably the tip of the iceberg."
The criminal complaint against Alfozan does not allege that Raed or its other partners were aware of Alfozan allegedly planting a recording device at OpenAI.
The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California, according to the Department of Justice.
Alfozan is charged in U.S. District Court in San Francisco with one count of using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.
He is being detained pending an Oct. 19 detention hearing, where his lawyer could argue for his release on bond. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, DOJ said.
Alfozan is not charged with corporate espionage or stealing trade secrets.
OpenAI earlier this year held discussions with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the country's sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the AI company.
Raed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNBC has also requested comment from the Saudi embassy in Washington.
Alfozan's criminal defense attorney, William Pernik, told CNBC by email, "At this point, the information provided has been extremely limited, as the charging documents have just been unsealed yesterday."
OpenAI declined to comment on Wednesday about whether it knew about Alfozan's position at the Saudi firm. And the company said it can't share more details about the conference room in question due to operational security concerns.
The company said in a post on X on Tuesday, "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
"We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,"
the company said. "Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
Alfozan, in a recent interview with the podcast Identity Capital about his career, noted that in July 2016, he and other Saudi nationals who were working at various tech companies in Silicon Valley met with their nation's now-de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The prince was visiting Silicon Valley as part of a U.S. tour to promote his "Vision 2030" economic diversification plan.
"One of the issues we discussed was whether we should move back to [the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia] now and bring our technical skills to improve the economy ... or should we work a few more years before we go back in order to gain more experience," Alfozan said in the interview, which was conducted in Arabic, translated by CNBC and posted online Sept. 24.
Bin Salman replied that "the country was undergoing major development and did not have the talent to train the next generation who would carry on those development plans," Alfozan said.
Alfozan added that the group of young workers "decided it was best to continue to learn and develop our skills before taking our knowledge back to [Saudi Arabia] to improve the tech sector."
Throughout the podcast, Alfozan discusses in detail his trajectory from coding in high school in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, to his career in the U.S. At one point in the interview, he refers to himself as an "introvert," who still pushes himself to help other young professionals find success in Silicon Valley.
Days after the podcast was posted, on Sept. 30, a federal criminal complaint alleges that OpenAI staff discovered "a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in" a conference room.
The device, which had a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage, was concealed in toilet paper, according to the complaint.
Alfozan had no authority to enter the conference room, which is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," according to the complaint.
The conference room can be reserved "only by executives and executive assistants," and is typically used "for internal leadership meetings and technical and product sessions, as well as external briefings with government officials and business counterparts," the complaint said.
Closed-circuit TV footage at OpenAI showed Alfozan close to the conference room on multiple days in September at various times, according to the complaint.
The filing also said that in August, and again in September, Alfozan used an AI productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, as well as "external partner meetings."
And a chatbot associated with Alfozan's spouse, which the complaint alleges shared several identifying characteristics with his own account, allegedly submitted detailed prompts about building, customizing, installing and remotely accessing a recording device. Alfozan's spouse, who was not identified in the complaint, has not been charged with any wrongdoing.
After the recording device was found hidden in the TV in the conference room, OpenAI placed a camera in that room, the complaint says.
Alfozan was seen on that camera entering the conference room at about 1:20 p.m. on Oct. 5, and "checking behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted," the complaint alleges.
That same day, the complaint said, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a printer room at OpenAI.
Inside that bag, OpenAI security found his wallet, ID and "another recording device" made by the same Chinese manufacturer, Seeed, which made the device found inserted in the conference room's TV, the complaint says.
The second recording device, like the first one, "had a recording microcontroller," and "had been customized to obfuscate anything stored on the device, such as potentially intercepted audio communications," the complaint said.
Alfozan reported to OpenAI that he had lost the bag, which was returned to him without the second recording device, according to the complaint. He did not inquire about the device, although he asked about certain other items that he said were missing, the complaint said.
"Any attempt to illicitly obtain protected information from U.S. super intelligence and technology companies threatens both American innovation and the national security interests those advancements support," Scott Schelble, special agent in charge of the FBI San Francisco Field Office, said in a statement on Tuesday about Alfozan's arrest, using the Trump administration's preferred term for artificial intelligence.
Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan had a long track record of work experience in the Bay Area.
On his LinkedIn page, Alfozan describes himself as an "Experienced Engineering Lead with 11 years of building scalable and reliable software systems in the data and AI/ML domains."
"Proven track record of leading engineering teams, delivering complex projects and enterprise products.
Driven by strong project management skills and a passion for cultivating a culture of collaboration and engineering excellence," his bio there says.
Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan was a founding engineer at Nash, an AI firm focused on logistics, according to his LinkedIn page.
And prior to Nash, he worked as a senior systems engineer at Facebook's parent company, Meta, from 2017 through 2022, according to his LinkedIn page. His internships before that included one at Microsoft in 2014, his bio says.
Alfozan studied computer science and engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and data science at the University of California, Berkeley, according to his LinkedIn page.
MIT's media relations office said he was enrolled there from January 2011 through January 2014, and again from February 2016 through May 2016, without receiving a degree.
A UC Berkeley spokesperson said Alfozan attended the school from January 2023 through May 2025, and earned a master's degree.
In 2016, he was a research intern at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia, he said on LinkedIn.
In 2020, he won a $50,000 second prize in the Saudi Covid-19 Challenge, a hackathon event, according to the profile.
Alfozan's home, on a hill in Millbrae, California, overlooks San Francisco Bay with views of Mount Diablo. The small San Mateo County suburb, which is popular with tech workers, is located about 30 minutes south of San Francisco and 25 minutes from Stanford University. No one answered the doorbell of the home Wednesday when a CNBC reporter rang.
The Financial Times reported that Alfozan was "born in the ultraconservative central region of Qassim," but "grew up in Dammam in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province."
The FT also reported that in a documentary about Alfozan that aired on Saudi television, his father said that as a young student in a government-backed program for gifted children to develop skills in mathematics, physics and engineering, Alfozan "would read the encyclopedia cover to cover."
"We are waiting to see what evidence the government has against our client, and look forward to presenting all appropriate defenses in court," Pernik, Alfozan's attorney, said.
"What I can tell you by way of a statement is that, like countless Americans, Mr. Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream," the attorney said. "He spent years studying, working and contributing to an American technological sector that leads the world, a sector built in large part by immigrants like him."
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why," Pernik said.
The lawyer noted that Alfozan is "charged with violating a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent."
"There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us," Pernik said. "Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origins is — and always should be — a protected status under our system of laws."
— Ashley Capoot, Lora Kolodny and Reem Nasr contributed to this report.

Alfozan's home, on a hill in Millbrae, California, overlooks San Francisco Bay with views of Mount Diablo. The small San Mateo County suburb, which is popular with tech workers, is located about 30 minutes south of San Francisco and 25 minutes from Stanford University. No one answered the doorbell of the home Wednesday when a CNBC reporter rang.
The Financial Times reported that Alfozan was "born in the ultraconservative central region of Qassim," but "grew up in Dammam in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province."
The FT also reported that in a documentary about Alfozan that aired on Saudi television, his father said that as a young student in a government-backed program for gifted children to develop skills in mathematics, physics and engineering, Alfozan "would read the encyclopedia cover to cover."
"We are waiting to see what evidence the government has against our client, and look forward to presenting all appropriate defenses in court," Pernik, Alfozan's attorney, said.
"What I can tell you by way of a statement is that, like countless Americans, Mr. Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream," the attorney said. "He spent years studying, working and contributing to an American technological sector that leads the world, a sector built in large part by immigrants like him."
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why," Pernik said.
The lawyer noted that Alfozan is "charged with violating a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent."
"There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us," Pernik said. "Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origins is — and always should be — a protected status under our system of laws."

title: OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns
titleJa: OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns
summaryJa: OpenAI is facing mounting scrutiny over its safety and security practices, including around how the company is working to protect children.
bodyOriginal:
Eight states filed lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday alleging that the artificial intelligence company's ChatGPT chatbot is an unsafe product that's harmed children and deceived parents.
Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana have individually sued OpenAI in their own state courts, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a release. She said Iowa's lawsuit aims to "vindicate the rights of Iowans affected by OpenAI's willful, dangerous, reckless, and unlawful conduct."
"OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans," Bird said in a statement. "OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it's giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend. My lawsuit is about protecting our kids and holding OpenAI accountable under our state law."
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has built age-specific protections into its product that "many other AI products lack." He added that OpenAI is working with states to advance policies that will apply to the entire industry.
"While no system can be perfect, we'll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today," Pusateri said.
OpenAI is facing mounting scrutiny over its safety and security practices, including around how the company is working to protect children. In a number of wrongful death lawsuits, ChatGPT is blamed for driving users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also sued OpenAI in June, alleging the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users.
OpenAI has taken steps to enhance safety features for parents and children over the last year, and in August it launched a dedicated experience for minors called ChatGPT for Teens. That product includes a range of educational features and age-appropriate safeguards that are intended to reduce exposure to developmentally inappropriate or harmful content.
"Teens should be able to use AI to learn, create, and explore," OpenAI said in a release at the time. "But that access should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time."
If you are having suicidal thoughts or are in distress, contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 for support and assistance from a trained counselor.

title: Dell stock plunges 11%, leading data center sell-off as fears mount about 'enterprise AI timing'
titleJa: Dell stock plunges 11%, leading data center sell-off as fears mount about 'enterprise AI timing'
summaryJa: Barclays downgraded Dell, HPE, and NetApp on concerns that enterprise AI adoption is lagging.
bodyOriginal:
Dell shares plummeted 11% on Wednesday and dragged down other data center equipment names on mounting concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won't justify the AI buildout.
Hewlett-Packard Enterprise, Oracle and Super Micro all joined in the downward slide.
In a report to clients on Wednesday, analysts at Barclays downgraded its rating on Dell, HPE and NetApp, "after a significant run and on enterprise AI timing."
Makers of data center servers and other backend equipment have been favored on Wall Street this year on optimism that they'll be selling huge volumes of gear tied to demand for AI chips and systems for years into the future. Dell has been one of the top performers on the market, up more than 300% this year, while HPE has jumped about 160% and NetApp has doubled.
However, sentiment toward the AI infrastructure space has shifted of late due in part to concerning revenue figures out of OpenAI and more broadly out of fear that rising interest rates will create a challenging environment as so much of the buildout is reliant on debt. Oracle, a heavy borrower, dropped 9% on Wednesday and is now down 33% for the year while neocloud CoreWeave plunged 15%, wiping out its gains for 2026.
The Barclays analysts said they haven't seen a "meaningful AI inflection" when it comes to enterprise spending for Dell, HPE and NetApp, lowering the rating on each to the equivalent of a hold from buy. They instead attribute increased revenue to the global memory shortage and noted that infrastructure companies have passed the higher price of memory along to customers.
"There is growing sentiment about enterprise AI adoption creating a hardware refresh," the Barclays analysts wrote, adding that businesses are typically allocating just 5% of their IT budgets to AI. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time."
The Barclays analysts also found that only about a quarter of total enterprise AI spend is going towards hardware. They said normalizing and eventually declining memory prices could weigh on infrastructure-related revenue.
Memory is a notoriously cyclical business, and stocks were hit this week after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress over the weekend on a new chip structure. Micron is down 11% for the week, while South Korea's SK Hynix has tumbled 13% in U.S. trading and Western Digital has dropped more than 8%.

title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
titleJa: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
summaryJa: Confirming the review, the government said it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".
bodyOriginal:
Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
- Published
Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.
Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10.
Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.
The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".
The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".
'Rip-off'
The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers".
"We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC.
"Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do."
The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis.
Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year.
None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC.
It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports.
Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest
- Published23 July
Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport.
"Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports.
She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution".
The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports.
Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households.

title: How high inflation became a 'fact of life' in the U.S.
titleJa: How high inflation became a 'fact of life' in the U.S.
summaryJa: U.S. inflation has stayed elevated for years, raising concern at the Federal Reserve that consumers may come to expect stubbornly high prices.
bodyOriginal:
U.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest stretches of elevated inflation of the past century. Some are beginning to act like it's a new normal, raising alarm bells for members of the Federal Reserve.
Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a 3.7% increase year over year in September. CPI has now registered around 65 months — that's more than five years — of consecutive annual readings above 2%, a widely accepted target for inflation in the U.S.
This yearslong spell of high inflation has cast a dark cloud over everyday Americans' view of the economy, and could shape everything from how they budget to how they vote in next month's midterm elections. At the Fed, leaders are left questioning whether consumers' inflationary expectations are becoming too entrenched to rein in.
"They're starting to accept high inflation as just a fact of life," Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wrote in a social media post last week. "That's concerning."
Inflation by the numbers
The current streak of stubborn inflation ranks among the most persistent in modern U.S. history.
The uninterrupted string of above-2% monthly CPI readings is the longest of the 21st century, according to a CNBC analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. has seen longer periods on only two other occasions going back to the late 1940s.
Since inflation started running above 2% in early 2021, the average CPI reading has sat around 4.5%. The last time a streak had a mean reading that high was during a period ending in the 1980s.
Consumers are expecting inflation to accelerate. The one-year inflation outlook in September rose three-tenths of a percentage point to 3.9%, its highest reading in more than three years, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations released last week.
How consumers respond
One of the main worries of central bankers is that businesses and consumers may start permanently adjusting their behaviors to account for high prices. That can have ripple effects through the economy.
Businesses anticipating rising costs can preemptively hike prices for consumers. Workers expecting sticky inflation will ask for steeper pay raises to get ahead of any sticker shock.
All of this can make inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy, rendering the monetary policy tools at the Fed's disposal less effective in slowing price growth.
"Inflation expectations have to be anchored for monetary policy to affect the economy in an effective and predictable manner," said Gary Richardson, an economist and former historian at the Fed. "That's got to be number-one goal of any central bank."
At this juncture, Fed officials are closely watching to see if and how consumers respond to inflationary pressures.
During an event last month, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he heard from a labor union leader that inflation was "worse" than a recession for their members. Kashkari said that conversation influenced how he views the trade-off within the Fed's so-called dual mandate, which calls for stability in prices and maximum employment.
At a gathering of economists in Ohio this week, Hammack told the audience that she did not take the fact that long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored "for granted." With each month that inflation comes in high, she warned that the risk grows of an "inflationary mindset" getting entrenched.
Economists widely view interest rate hikes as the Fed's main mechanism for slowing demand and, in turn, putting downward pressure on the annual pace of price growth. After hiking interest rates in September, Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs further in December and in 2027.
In the long run, Diane Swonk, chief economist at consultancy KPMG, said interest rate hikes can benefit consumers by getting inflation under control. But in the near term, Swonk said consumers can feel more pressure due to higher borrowing costs.
"Inflation is like a cancer, and if you let it metastasize and go further, it's even worse," Swonk said. "Even when the cure hurts, it's better than letting it metastasize."
Unhappy shoppers
In Hammack's district, the Cleveland Fed chief said via social media that she's found evidence that residents are "choosing" rather than "trading down." For instance, she said they need to pick whether to pay for groceries or essential bills.
Consumers have lamented the cumulative price increases they now see in everyday life after the years-long run of high inflation. Adding to their woes is the fact that year-over-year inflation has run at a faster clip than wage growth in recent months, meaning the average consumer has lost purchasing power.
The University of Michigan's closely followed consumer sentiment survey earlier this year fell to the lowest levels ever seen. The highest share of respondents citing high prices as a reason for having worse personal finances surpassed 50% for the first time on record in 2026.
High prices are "dominating consumer thinking," said Joanne Hsu, the director of Michigan's survey. "They still consider it an unacceptable fact of life."
Compared with Democrats, consumer sentiment has tumbled more sharply among Republicans and independents this year. The question now is if voters angered about the rising cost of living will shift control in Washington away from Republicans and President Donald Trump in the midterm election.
Despite those glum outlooks, economists say that everyday Americans shouldn't bank on prices coming down from current levels. Deflation — which is when annual price growth falls below 0% — could put the national economy on a downward spiral.
Instead, their hope should be that inflation's 12-month growth rate can cool to levels below the pace of pay increases. If that happens for a long enough period, the higher wages and increased purchasing power would leave shoppers better equipped for today's prices.
Olena Nicks, an analyst and local lawmaker in Long Island, New York, is one of those consumers tightening the purse strings in the face of lofty prices. Nicks said she's specifically noticed steep price increases over recent years in the grocery store produce aisle and when looking at airline flights for vacations.
In response, the 34-year-old said she's cut back on purchasing meals at restaurants or from fast-food chains. Her friend group has forgone leisure activities like bowling, opting instead for less-costly nights spent in someone's home.
"Frustrated is an understatement," Nicks said. "It feels like you're stuck."

High prices are "dominating consumer thinking," said Joanne Hsu, the director of Michigan's survey. "They still consider it an unacceptable fact of life."
Compared with Democrats, consumer sentiment has tumbled more sharply among Republicans and independents this year. The question now is if voters angered about the rising cost of living will shift control in Washington away from Republicans and President Donald Trump in the midterm election.
Despite those glum outlooks, economists say that everyday Americans shouldn't bank on prices coming down from current levels. Deflation — which is when annual price growth falls below 0% — could put the national economy on a downward spiral.
Instead, their hope should be that inflation's 12-month growth rate can cool to levels below the pace of pay increases. If that happens for a long enough period, the higher wages and increased purchasing power would leave shoppers better equipped for today's prices.

title: Fannie Mae sharply raises mortgage rate forecast for 2027
titleJa: Fannie Mae sharply raises mortgage rate forecast for 2027
summaryJa: Fannie Mae just put out its latest forecast for mortgage rates, and they are much higher than previous estimates.
bodyOriginal:
Economists at Fannie Mae are now predicting much higher mortgage rates through the end of 2026 and into 2027. It now puts the average rate on the 30-year fixed at 7.4% for the fourth quarter of this year and 7.5% through all of next year. It previously forecast 6.8% for the fourth quarter and 6.7% for all of next year.
The average rate on the 30-year fixed stood at 7.46% Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily, but will likely move higher today. Bond yields are rising after a hotter-than-expected inflation report.
Mortgage rates have been rising sharply since the start of September, as inflation remains stubbornly high and bond markets sell off due to several factors. The Federal Reserve also raised its benchmark rate for the first time in more than three years. Mortgage rates do not follow the Fed's rate exactly, but they do react to how the central bank sees inflation going forward.
Mortgage rates loosely follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which has been rising sharply on higher oil prices and growing concerns in the global economy.

Pending sales, counted by signed contracts on existing homes, were down 8.5% in September year-over-year, according to Zillow. Mortgage demand continues to drop sharply, as buyers face higher prices and weakening affordability. Not only can fewer buyers now afford a home, but fewer can qualify for a mortgage.
Fannie Mae did not respond to requests for comment on its latest forecast.

title: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services
titleJa: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services
summaryJa: New Treasury Department findings may lend weight to President Donald Trump’s long-running grievance that major banks have discriminated against conservatives.
bodyOriginal:
The Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency found some of the largest banks serving the U.S. allowed political considerations, public pressure and social concerns to influence decisions about who received banking services, according to a sweeping report released Wednesday.
The OCC said it reviewed the nine largest national banks under its supervision, examining nearly 100,000 complaints and about 420,000 pages of documents. It found that all nine had used "reputation risk" policies that lacked "clear," "objective" standards and could disadvantage customers because of their political or religious views or lawful business activities.
"Banks should make decisions based on financial risk, not the political or social preferences of their employees or executives," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, according to a transcript of his in remarks Wednesday in Lexington, Kentucky.
The findings may lend new regulatory weight to a grievance President Donald Trump has pressed since returning to office. Trump has repeatedly accused and sued major banks for discriminating against conservatives and has said he was personally "debanked" after the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection, claims banks have denied.
The report lands a day after the OCC and other Treasury regulators imposed more than $1.2 billion in penalties on Bank of America over separate anti-money-laundering failures. At the same time, the OCC said it is examining whether banks' efforts to comply with anti-money-laundering rules have themselves contributed to debanking.
The review covered JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank and BMO Bank, which together held a majority of assets at OCC-supervised commercial banks when the probe began last year under a Trump executive order.
The OCC stopped short of announcing fines or sanctions Wednesday, but said it is considering additional rules aimed at preventing political or religious discrimination.
Among the cases it highlighted: JPMorgan subsidiary WePay closed accounts belonging to merchants selling Trump and conservative merchandise. An internal screening list included terms such as "MAGA," "Make America Great" and "America First," even though the OCC found neither WePay nor JPMorgan had formal written standards for deciding when flagged material amounted to prohibited hate or violence.
JPMorgan told CNBC its policies prohibit discrimination based on political or religious views and said WePay's process "did not meet our expectations." The bank said it fixed the issue and has since shut down the business.
"We are not forcing these banks to serve every customer," Gould said. "Instead, banks should evaluate every customer on objective, risk-based criteria."
The other banks did not immediately respond to request for comment.
The report also found examples cutting the other way politically.
Capital One declined relationships with an abortion-rights group after noting that about 95% of its political contributions went to Democrats, and with a public education group whose political arm endorsed only Democratic candidates. It also passed on a gun-rights group over concerns that banking it could look like an endorsement.
The practices extended beyond overtly political groups too, the report indicates.
The OCC found restrictions affecting firearms, fossil fuels, private prisons, tobacco and cryptocurrency, and said some banks' appetite for those businesses shifted with the political climate — risking a "whipsaw" effect between administrations.
All nine banks told the OCC they have since revised or consolidated policies aimed at ensuring fair access. But the regulator said none has fully acknowledged past debanking decisions or created a comprehensive program to remediate affected customers.

title: Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff in steepest cuts since 2022
titleJa: Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff in steepest cuts since 2022
summaryJa: The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide.
bodyOriginal:
Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff in steepest cuts since 2022
- Published
Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.
The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.
Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".
The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.
In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".
Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.
Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."
Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".
The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.
Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.
The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.
It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.
However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.
He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau.
"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.
The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
titleJa: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
summaryJa: Iran has escalated its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks, as it tries to choke off a rebound in crude oil exports.
bodyOriginal:
A container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday as Iran escalated its attacks on commercial vessels.
The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore.
"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early Wednesday that a container ship exploded and sank after hitting a naval mine, according to the state news agency Tasnim. But there is no independent evidence to confirm that a mine is what caused the Pride to sink, according to the maritime security firm Marisks.
Iran's claims are "consistent with an ongoing psychological operations campaign aimed at generating fear, increasing uncertainty and discouraging commercial shipping" in Hormuz, Marisks said in a security alert.
Iran has escalated its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks, as it tries to choke off a rebound in crude oil exports through the strait.
More than 20 vessels, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack this month in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
The attacks this month have left two sailors missing and 12 injured, according to the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations' agency.
Crude oil exports through Hormuz hit prewar levels in September as the U.S. military guided tankers through the strait, but shipments have since pulled back as attacks have increased.
Crude exports through Hormuz averaged 8.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week ended Oct. 12, nearly 40% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler.
Shipments from the entire region, including pipelines to the Gulf of Oman and Red Sea, stood at 14 million bpd, or nearly 20% below prewar levels, the data showed.
Daily flows are volatile, with only 3 million barrels of crude transiting Hormuz on Monday while 6 million barrels passed through the strait on Friday, according to Kpler.

titleJa: CoreWeave shares tumble as bond yields near 15% on concern about AI borrowing binge
summaryJa: CoreWeave's stock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the artificial intelligence build-out.Shares of the so-called neocloud nosedived 16%, while yields on its debt jumped higher. The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 is sitting at 14.8%, while that of its 9.75% bond due in 2031 is around 14.9%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
bodyOriginal:
CoreWeave's stock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the artificial intelligence build-out.
Shares of the so-called neocloud nosedived 16%, while yields on its debt jumped higher. The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 is sitting at 14.8%, while that of its 9.75% bond due in 2031 is around 14.9%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
While investors were once excited about getting in on the AI action, investor sentiment has started to shift, said Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
Now, investors are demanding more risk compensation, he said.
"The era of easy money, which we experienced in the first nine months of the year, is starting to disappear and dissipate," Alvarado noted. "Now the extra dollar or the marginal dollar is going to be more looked at with a microscope into the concessions that the issuer is giving you back."
Tech investor Chamath Palihapitiya, founder and CEO of investment firm Social Capital and CEO of AI company 8090, called out the soaring yields on X late Tuesday. That prompted Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to respond, "yikes."
Palihapitiya shared a chart of the 2032 bond, noting that the yield "touched 15%" and then "closed at a new high" on Tuesday. He also included part of his deep dive into whether the AI build-out is creating a private credit bubble, in which he noted "how little extra lenders appear to charge for AI risk."
Tech sector hit
CoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. For instance, shares of Oracle tumbled nearly 7% on Wednesday. Yields on its bonds were also higher, with the yield to maturity on its 6.25% bond due in Nov. 2032 sitting at 7.24%.
The overall tech sector brought down the stock market on Wednesday with the Nasdaq Composite losing 1.4%. The debt concern seems to be hitting the shakier stocks outside of the "Magnificent Seven" the hardest.
Another neocloud stock, Nebius, dropped 9%.
Companies are in a race to build AI infrastructure and have turned to the credit market to finance their projects, leading to a jump in supply. Dell cratered by 10%.
Overall, hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion this year, according to JPMorgan. By 2027, it is expected to exceed $1 trillion annually, the bank said.

title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
titleJa: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
summaryJa: Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI.
bodyOriginal:
Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
- Published
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
But, here's we do know so far.
Help from a chatbot
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.
The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
Hiding in plain toilet paper
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan?
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."
Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."
On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.
